title: 2 Samuel 3:1–5
context: After Asahel’s death at Gibeon, the conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David settles into a long war. The narrator sums it up in a single contrast: David’s house grows stronger while Saul’s house grows weaker. He then pauses to list six sons born to David in Hebron, each by a different mother. The list marks David’s growing household and status, and it also introduces names that will matter greatly later in the book, especially Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah. Both traditions read the passage as a quiet record of God’s purpose advancing through ordinary politics and family life, with seeds of later sorrow already present.

verses.text: Now there was a long war between Saul’s house and David’s house. David grew stronger and stronger, but Saul’s house grew weaker and weaker.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the long war is described as a real struggle between two houses, with human loyalties, choices, and battles shaping its course over time. David’s rise is not instant; it unfolds gradually as people and leaders decide whom they will follow, and the narrative takes those decisions seriously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the steady contrast between David’s strengthening and Saul’s weakening as the outworking of what God had already declared when he rejected Saul and chose David (1 Samuel 15–16). Both traditions agree that God’s purpose moves forward here through slow, ordinary historical processes rather than sudden miracle.

verses.text: Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the list of sons begins with Amnon, whose later conduct will bring grief to David’s house (2 Samuel 13). Placing his name first, without comment, lets the reader recognize later that blessings like a growing family carry real responsibility, and that what people do with such gifts matters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that sons born in Hebron are a sign of David’s establishment as a king with a dynasty, a theme that will come to full expression in the LORD’s promise of a lasting house (2 Samuel 7). Both traditions recognize that the same family that signals blessing will also become the scene of much of David’s later sorrow.

verses.text: and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Chileab, son of Abigail, is otherwise almost unmentioned, while Absalom, son of Maacah, will later lead a rebellion against his father. The list holds together sons whose stories go very differently, a reminder that each person in the household will answer for his own path.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Absalom’s mother is a daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, which suggests a marriage with political dimensions; Geshur will later shelter Absalom (2 Samuel 13:37–38). Both traditions see the narrator laying groundwork for later events, with God’s purposes running through a household of mixed motives and alliances.

verses.text: and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Adonijah, son of Haggith, will later attempt to take the throne before Solomon (1 Kings 1). His appearance here as the fourth son highlights how questions of succession grow out of the ordinary facts of birth order, ambition, and choice within David’s large family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Shephatiah and Adonijah are named alongside the others without any hint of who will finally inherit the throne. The eventual king, Solomon, is not on this list at all, and both traditions see this as a reminder that God’s choice of David’s successor does not simply follow birth order.

verses.text: and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David’s wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the list closes with Ithream, son of Eglah, and repeats that all six were born in Hebron. The multiplication of wives reflects the royal customs of the time, and many readers set it beside the warning that a king should not multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), letting the reader weigh David’s choices honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the tension between David’s many marriages and the Deuteronomic warning, and see the narrator recording facts that will bear bitter fruit without excusing them. Both traditions agree that the Bible presents David as God’s chosen king while refusing to present his household as a model to imitate.
